routes.overview: New York Gully splits the NW Face of Snoqualmie Mountain, the most-climbed of five parallel ice/mixed lines on that wall (alongside Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, and LA Express). First climbed by Ruch and Cordery-Cotter in 1985 as a IV 5.8 A2 WI4 aid line, it's a roughly 700-ft alpine route following a prominent gully system to a distinctive 'box gully' feature, finishing with a steep corner pitch that was originally aided and first freed in 2004 at M5+/6-.
routes.beta: A popular Seattle-area winter mixed testpiece: a short approach off I-90 leads to a moderate lower gully, then progressively steeper mixed ground (up to M5-) through slabby, sometimes loose rock, finishing at a splitter 5.8 corner crack that was historically aided (A1-2) and has since been free-climbed. Conditions vary widely year to year — some seasons build fat ice through the gully, dry years leave it mostly rock/mixed with minimal screw placements. It sits on the edge of the Phantom Slide avalanche path, so timing relative to snowpack stability is as important as the climbing itself.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting based on remaining daylight, current avalanche danger on the Phantom Slide approach/exit, and how the party is moving on the mixed pitches — this is a committing gully route with limited fast bail options above the crux, so err toward retreating early if conditions, ice quality, or teammate pace are below expectations rather than pushing into the crux pitch late in the day.

routes.descent: From the top, most parties rappel from a tree anchor at a col between two gendarmes into the Enigma Gully (Slot couloir), then climb snow back up to the main summit ridge near 6,200 ft and walk the last bit to the summit. From there, descend the standard Southwest Slopes scramble route back to the Source Lake/Alpental trail, or, snow permitting, ski or boot back down the Phantom Slide to the resort. Round trip is commonly 8-11 hours car-to-car.

routes.detailed_rack: A single 60m rope plus a thin tag line (or a single 70m rope for simul-climbing sections) is standard. Rack to 2-3 inches including offset nuts and cams in the 0.2-0.5 in range for the P4/P5 dihedral and crack systems, a few knifeblade pitons for thin seams, and 3-4 ice screws (10-13cm) — screw count and size needs vary hugely with conditions, from essentially unnecessary in dry years to fully useful in a fat-ice season. No bolts on route; some fixed pitons exist at select stances. Bring extra slings for tree/horn anchors on the lower gully and for the walk-off.
what_to_bring: Extra insulating layers for cold, shaded belays
Avalanche gear (beacon/shovel/probe) for the Phantom Slide crossing
Approach footwear or light snowshoes for the initial hillside
pro_tips: Time the Phantom Slide crossing for early morning when the snowpack is most consolidated
Check recent trip reports before committing — ice coverage on this NW aspect varies drastically year to year

Phantom Slide approach crosses active avalanche path — check NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast, time crossing for safety

routes.pro_needs: Protection is a mix of thin-crack gear (offsets, small cams, knifeblades) for the rock sections and screws for whatever ice is present that season; the crux corner crack takes good small-to-medium cams and was historically bridged with two moves of fixed-gear aid (A1-2) before being freed.
routes.best_season: Best after a solid early/mid-winter freeze builds ice in the box gully and the upper corner; a sustained cold snap in Dec-Jan usually gives the fattest ice, while warm or dry winters can leave the route thin, forcing dry-tooling on rock (per 2025 trip reports). The northwest aspect stays cold and holds what ice forms later into the season than sunnier Cascade lines.
routes.approach: Park in the Alpental groomer lot, about 200 ft past the main day-lot at the end of WA-906/Alpental Rd (reached via I-90 Exit 52). From the lot, walk up the open, south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the base of the falls, cut left into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb up through two steep, often snowed-up rock/cliff bands — this section is frequently booted or skinned by prior parties, and picking up an existing track through the thick timber makes a real difference in speed and route-finding; without one, expect slow going. After about 300 ft of gain, angle right onto the Phantom Slide itself, a broad avalanche path that is the defining feature (and hazard) of this approach: it slides regularly, including on skiers and climbers on the upper apron, so check the NWAC forecast beforehand and time your crossing/ascent to stable conditions rather than lingering on it. Climb the slide path to about 4,900 ft, then trend left and up through lower-angle, more open terrain to a notch on the NW shoulder/West Ridge near 5,200 ft. From the notch, downclimb roughly 200 vertical feet into the Thunder Creek cirque basin and traverse beneath the NW Face to the base of the gully system — note this face hosts five closely spaced ice/mixed lines (Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully, and LA Express), so confirm you're racking up below the correct one. No reliable water source along this approach in winter/spring conditions; plan to melt snow. Figure roughly 1.5–3 hours car-to-base depending on snowpack, track conditions, and party experience with the terrain.
routes.descent_text: From the top of the technical climbing (the crux mixed pitches, including the route's namesake 'box gully' section), downclimb easy snow angling to climber's right, then traverse up to a col between two gendarmes on the upper ridge. From that col, make one rappel from an established tree anchor — a single 60m rope reaches the bottom comfortably (many parties carry a 70m since it's also useful for simul-climbing/leading the route's 4 long pitches), dropping into the Enigma Gully, also known locally as the Slot couloir. This tree-anchor rappel is also the standard bail point if weather, conditions, or time force a retreat before topping out. From the base of the rappel, climb back up moderate snow in the Enigma/Slot gully to regain the main summit ridge near 6,200 ft, then walk the short remaining distance to Snoqualmie Mountain's true summit. From the summit, descend the standard Southwest Slopes scramble route: steep, loose scree and exposed rock past Cave Ridge, dropping toward the Source Lake basin and rejoining the Snow Lake/Source Lake trail back to the Alpental parking lot (this standard descent line is roughly 3,100 ft of its own elevation loss over about 1.9 miles one-way, and is considered a genuinely hard, sustained scramble in its own right, not just a walk-down). In good, stable snow conditions some parties instead ski or boot straight back down the Phantom Slide to the resort rather than taking the scree-and-scramble Southwest Slopes line. Total rappels on route: 1. Round trip is commonly 8–11 hours car-to-car.
routes.bail: The col rappel into the Enigma Gully can be used to bail before the crux pitch; lower on the route, parties can generally downclimb/retreat the approach gully back toward the Phantom Slide in stable conditions.

pitch_detail.notes: Follows a snow gully/bench just below a rocky bulge with a steep drop below; often simul-climbed with pitch 2.
Traverses up and left across the face on thin snow over rock to a short snow/rock gully ending at a dead snag below the box gully.
The 'box gully' crux: climbs straight up through a 3-sided box cave feature protected by pins and cams; the crux corner above was originally aided and first freed in 2004 at M5+/6-.
A short ice step (takes a 10cm screw) leads to a traverse across a snow ledge to a fixed multi-piece anchor.

days.note: Climbed car-to-car in a single long day. Parties hike from the Alpental lot up past the waterfalls through two steep snowed-up cliff bands to the base of the gully (the 'Phantom Slide' approach), then climb 4-6 pitches of ice/mixed/snow (crux typically a mixed step in the M4-M5 range) to a col below the summit ridge. From there most parties rappel from a tree anchor into Enigma Gully (the Slot Couloir), climb the snow back up, and descend the standard southwest slopes to the car.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the notch, downclimb about 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

Why that matters here more than anywhere else on this page: this face carries five closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

The pitch-one confirmation, and it is a good one: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an obvious ramp out to the left, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

The second confirmation is higher and unambiguous: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a small headwall split by a 5.8 crack, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

And a honest warning about the approach itself: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.

hazards: Loose, detached blocks throughout the chimney
routes.overview: A short, single-pitch mixed chimney climb just right of the Snot Couloir on Snoqualmie Mountain's northwest face.
routes.beta: Climbs a left-leaning open chimney choked with mostly large and medium blocks. Start from a snowy ledge about 7 ft up, then traverse left using staircase footwork; the route offers chimney-stemming or face-climbing variations around detached blocks. The crux comes near the top in a constriction holding a large chockstone, though an optional left traverse bypasses it.
routes.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.2 to #3 plus nuts; abundant protection options throughout the pitch.
pro_tips: An optional left traverse near the top bypasses the chockstone crux.
watch_out: The chimney is filled with large and medium loose/detached blocks.
routes.pro_needs: Standard single-pitch trad rack; plentiful placements.
routes.best_season: Winter-spring, alongside the face's other mixed/ice lines.
routes.approach: Same NW-face approach as New York Gully; the route sits just right of the end of the Snot Couloir, around the end of the ridge that divides the right side of the NW Face.

routes.overview: A steep, sustained mixed ice line on Snoqualmie Mountain's northwest face featuring a distinctive ice/snow cave (the route's namesake 'snostril'), finishing near the Thunder Basin exit gully.
routes.beta: Adds another quality mixed line to the NW Face alongside New York Gully. Pitch 1 climbs slabby ice (can be split into two shorter pitches). Pitch 2 is thin, steep ice and mixed ground leading to the cave entrance. Pitch 3 traverses right to an overhanging mixed wall to a rock belay. Pitch 4 climbs a snow couloir up to about 55°. Pitch 5 either continues to a saddle or takes the recommended "Post Nasal Drip" mixed variation.

waypoints.name: The Snostril (NW Face)
waypoints.directions: Approach as for New York Gully: climb the slope above the lots toward the Alpental waterfalls, go left into the woods below them and straight up through two steep cliff bands, then move right to the edge of the Phantom Slide path and climb it to about 4,900 ft. Continue up and left through a lower-angled clearing to a notch in the west ridge at about 5,200 ft, then downclimb the gully on its north side, a couple hundred feet at about 45 degrees, into the Thunder Creek cirque below the northwest face. The route starts in a corner just right of a large cave, roughly halfway between the Thunder Basin exit gully and the Snot Couloir.

routes.detailed_rack: A single rack to a #4 Camalot plus a full ice-screw complement — both cams and screws are needed.
pro_tips: Study New York Gully's approach and aerial photos of the NW Face before you go to find the start.
The "Post Nasal Drip" finish (WI4 M5) is the recommended variation over the easier walk-off finish to the saddle.
watch_out: Sustained, technical mixed climbing with limited protection on some pitches
routes.pro_needs: Mixed protection: rock cams to #4 for the rock sections and ice screws for the ice pitches.
routes.best_season: Winter-spring, while ice and snow cover the mixed terrain and cave feature.
routes.approach: Same NW-face approach as New York Gully via the Phantom Slide path. Pitch 1 starts in a corner roughly halfway between the Thunder Basin exit gully and the Snot Couloir; cross-reference New York Gully's approach beta and aerial photos of the face to find the start.
routes.descent_text: Top out on the western subsummit and walk off down the steep south side, a snow slope in winter, then circle back to wherever you left packs below the face. If the crux above the cave is not in, rappel the first two pitches from the cave instead.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts on lower-angle ice just right of a large cave, in a corner roughly halfway between the Thunder Basin exit gully and the Snot Couloir — the last major weakness before the Snot. Slabby ice that is often thin, taking occasional rock gear; a mid-pitch stance lets it be split into two shorter pitches.

Thinner, steeper ice, sometimes all ice and sometimes with an occasional mixed move, climbs into the high cave (the 'snostril') beneath a huge chockstone. A full rope length or slightly more; belay inside the cave. If the crux above is not in, these two pitches still make a worthwhile ice outing with a retreat from here.

The crux: traverse right out of the cave onto an overhanging mixed wall, then finish on easier snow at the foot of a large couloir. Grades given range from WI4 M5 to WI4+ M5+ and shift with how much snow and ice has formed. Cams and screws are both needed; belay on rock on the left wall.

Climb the snow couloir above the cave at up to about 55°; parties often simul-climb the lower part. The Post Nasal Drip finish climbs the couloir's left wall above, so watch for it before continuing to the saddle.

The recommended finish is the Post Nasal Drip variation, a steep ice-and-mixed line up the couloir's left wall that often holds the best pure ice on the route. Alternatively continue up the moderate snow couloir, about 45 m, to the saddle. Top out on a western subsummit and descend a steep walk-off down the south side.

routes.overview: Chair Peak's North Face is one of Washington's most popular winter alpine ice-and-mixed classics, easily reached from Snoqualmie Pass. A moderate face of snow, ice, and mixed steps gives a superb, accessible introduction to winter alpine climbing when conditions are right.
routes.beta: Reached via a short traverse from the Source Lake-Snow Lake divide, the North Face offers about four pitches of steep snow and ice climbing on generally moderate-angle terrain (50-65°) with one short crux step that can approach 80° (sometimes rock, 5.4-5.6, if thin on ice). Abundant natural/fixed protection and a short approach make it a popular introduction to Cascade ice climbing, though it backs up with parties on clear winter weekends. Note: a distinct, harder rock variation called 'North Face Direct' (5.9, 5 pitches) starts about 200m from the standard line and should not be confused with this route.
routes.turnaround: Turn around if avalanche conditions or visibility deteriorate; winter days are short.
routes.rappels: Typically a single 60m rappel (occasionally two) through the summit gully/notch back into the basin; some late-day/crowded ascents have required additional downclimbing when rope length fell short
routes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
routes.descent: Descend the standard route / gully off the back toward the Snoqualmie Pass approach.

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-serve day-use fee kiosk (Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day); trail departs the north end of the upper Alpental Ski Area parking lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 52 at Snoqualmie Pass, follow Alpental Road to its end, staying past the lower ski-area lots to the upper parking area.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Snow Lake Trail here on the unmaintained boot path toward Source Lake, a reliable water source in the Alpental Valley.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the valley trail and follow it up the South Fork Snoqualmie River — an old ski-area service road and cat track for the first half mile, then standard trail. It climbs gently through forest and avalanche-path brush for roughly a mile and a half with Chair Peak's north side in view ahead.

waypoints.name: Thumb Tack
waypoints.note: Prominent rock outcrop in the basin below Chair's east face; a common gear-cache and roping-up point before the final approach.
waypoints.directions: Cross the creek below Source Lake, which can be awkward at high flow, then climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque beneath Chair's east face. These slopes are the runouts below Chair, Snoqualmie Mountain and The Tooth, so move through them early and without stopping.

waypoints.name: North Face open-book base
waypoints.note: Left-facing open book in the center of the north face where the route begins; three pitches of 50-70 degree snow/ice.
waypoints.directions: From the outcrop head north and climb the gully toward the northeast ridge rather than taking the northeast slopes direct; this gully is a known avalanche path with a fatal history. Follow the ridge around onto the north face and traverse the talus and snow apron below it to the open book, which sits roughly halfway across the face. A moat can open at the base of the ice later in the season and complicate the last few metres.

waypoints.name: Col below summit block
waypoints.note: Small col reached after the ice pitches; a crux step up to roughly 80 degrees (occasionally bare 5.6 rock) leads to the summit from here.
waypoints.directions: Four pitches up the face. Ice bulges to about 70 degrees off the base, then two rope-lengths of sustained snow and easy mixed ground belayed off scrub trees, then a final steepening to the col. Stay on the centre line — the ground off to climber's right is thin and downsloping slab. The last belay sits close to the ridge crest, which is often corniced.

waypoints.name: Chair Peak summit
waypoints.note: Small summit block; the northeast side is heavily corniced in winter, stay toward the uncorniced center.
waypoints.directions: A short, steep step above the col — sometimes bare rock when the ice is thin — leads to roughly 20 feet of blocky scrambling, normally done unroped. Keep well off the northeast lip on the last moves.

waypoints.name: South-side gully rappels
waypoints.note: Descend via rappels down the gully on the south side of the east face; watch for parties and loose rock/ice falling from above.
waypoints.directions: Leave the summit over the false summit and head east down the standard descent gully to a notch in the southeast ridge; the rappel line drops from there into the east-face basin. Anchors are natural — trees, horns and slings — so carry cord and webbing to back up or replace what you find. Expect a mix of downclimbing and one or two double-rope rappels depending on how much snow is in the gully.

routes.detailed_rack: A few ice screws (3-4), 2-3 pickets, slings for frequent tree-anchor belays on P2/P3, and a couple of small rock pieces or pitons for the crux step; two tools and crampons are mandatory.
pro_tips: Check the NWAC avalanche forecast — the approach and face are avalanche terrain.
Go when the ice is in; conditions vary widely through winter.
Watch the summit cornice on exit.
The crux is a short (~10 ft) step below the summit block that can hit ~80°; it's sometimes bare 5.6 rock rather than ice, so be ready to climb it either way.
Start near the left-facing open book in the center of the face; the four moderate pitches below the crux rely mainly on tree belays rather than screws.
routes.pro_needs: Screws, pickets, and a few rock pieces for the mixed step(s).
routes.best_season: December through March; early season is often unconsolidated snow over rock, with more consistent ice building through the freeze-thaw cycles of January-March.
routes.approach: Park at the upper Alpental parking lot (end of Alpental Road, shared with the Snow Lake / Source Lake trailhead). Pick up the maintained Alpental Valley trail, which runs along and above the South Fork Snoqualmie River on the old ski-area service road/cat track for about the first 0.5 mile before narrowing to a standard trail. Continue up-valley roughly 1.5-2 miles, climbing gently through forest and avalanche-path brush with Chair Peak's north side visible ahead; a boot path forks off the main Source Lake/Snow Lake trail toward Source Lake and the basin below Chair Peak's east/north aspect (~4200 ft). From the basin, ascend talus and (in season) a snow apron directly toward the base of the north face at the head of the Alpental cirque, aiming for the obvious snow/ice runnel system below the summit block. Total approach gain to the base is roughly 2,400 ft over about 2.5-3 miles one-way. Hazards: the valley floor and lower slopes cross active avalanche paths below Chair Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain, and The Tooth, so this is a serious slide-prone approach in winter/spring — most parties go early and move quickly through the runout zones; there is also a creek crossing near Source Lake that can be tricky at high flow, and the basin below the face holds a moat late-season that can complicate the final approach to the ice.
routes.descent_text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.
routes.bail: Down-climb or rappel off screws/pickets/rock; the face is moderate but conditions-dependent.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at the bergschrund/base of the face and climbs through a band of ice bulges on steepening ground up to roughly 70°; the center line generally holds better, more consolidated ice than the thin, downsloping rock slabs off to climber's right. Belay is built with screws once the angle eases on a shoulder partway up the face.

A full rope-length of sustained steep snow (roughly 50-60°) up the exposed face to a stout tree belay; conditions swing between firm neve good for standard axe placements and harder ice bulges that force a switch to front-pointing/piolet traction.

Moderate snow and mixed ground weaving past small rock bands, using scrub trees for protection and the belay; in fast, stable conditions parties commonly simul-climb this pitch together with pitch 2 rather than belaying it separately.

Steepens again to 50-70° snow and ice on the final headwall, sometimes including a short verglassed mixed/rock step, to a small col about 60 ft below the summit block; the belay sits near the often-corniced summit ridge, watch for cornice lip. From here it's an unroped scramble of about 20 ft of blocky rock to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Typically climbed as a winter/spring snow-and-ice route (roughly Dec-April); becomes rock/scree and much less appealing once it melts out by summer.

days.note: Standard winter/spring outing from the Alpental upper lot: hike/skin past Source Lake into the basin below Chair Peak, then climb 4 short pitches of snow/ice up the North Face gully to the notch and a short scramble to the summit. Most parties descend the standard (SE/backside) gully rather than reversing the face.

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the Thumb Tack, then over the northeast ridge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road. Head up the Alpental valley, on the old ski-area cat track for the first stretch and then on trail, toward Source Lake. The maintained tread effectively ends at Source Lake around 3,700-3,740 ft. If stability allows, climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque under Chair's east face, finishing at a freestanding rock called the Thumb Tack. That rock is the one unambiguous fix on the whole approach — use it as your reference, because everything above it is decided by aspect rather than by tread. From the Thumb Tack, go north up a gully to gain the Northeast Ridge. Take the gully rather than attacking the ridge directly from the northeast. This gully is a known avalanche path and has killed climbers. Once on the ridge, follow it to the buttress and round onto the north side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, below-freezing conditions after a thaw
hazards: the gully from the Thumb Tack to the northeast ridge is an avalanche path with a fatal accident history (two deaths in 1996)
avalanche paths cross the approach the length of the Alpental valley
route is only in condition below freezing after a thaw
moat at the base of the face late in the season

approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most important thing: the north face is not reached by climbing straight up the head of the Alpental cirque. You get onto it by crossing the northeast ridge first and coming round. A party grinding up the snow at the back of the cirque with the east face above them is under the wrong aspect entirely.

Once on the north side, the route starts roughly halfway across the face at a prominent open book — a corner with a gully feeding into it. Pitch one takes that corner on thin alpine ground; pitch two goes up steep snow and ice to a tree belay. The tree is your confirmation you picked the right corner.

If you are standing under a continuous, featureless snow apron with no corner system above it, you have stopped short — keep traversing across the face. If you are past the halfway point of the face with the summit block directly overhead, you have gone too far.

The route is only worth starting in below-freezing conditions, ideally after a thaw has consolidated the ice and snow; on the wrong day the corner is unprotectable slush over rock.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

routes.name: Northeast Buttress
routes.season: Dec-Mar (ice/mixed); also climbed as a rock scramble in summer
hazards: rockfall
variable rock quality
winter avalanche terrain
routes.overview: Chair Peak is the iconic chair-shaped summit at the head of the Alpental valley, one of the most recognizable peaks above Snoqualmie Pass. The northeast buttress is a classic moderate alpine rock climb, while the peak is equally famous as a winter mountaineering objective.
routes.beta: From the basin below Chair Peak's East Face, the route climbs a curving gully system on climber's right before trending up and left along the buttress crest to the summit. The technical crux in winter conditions is a short, steep ice bulge encountered partway up; in summer the route is straightforward exposed scrambling with occasional low-5th-class moves. It is commonly done in 4 pitches with a 60m rope, though many parties simul-climb sections or break it into 5-6 shorter pitches, especially in early-season snow. Short approach and moderate climbing make it very popular and prone to queues on clear winter weekends.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting based on daylight, crowding, and forecast warming - the descent gully is exposed to rockfall and cornice hazard that worsens as the day warms, so parties should plan to be off the upper mountain and through the gully before afternoon sun softens the snow and ice.
routes.rappels: 1-2 rope-length rappels (up to 60m) through the cornice-prone SW-facing exit gully, combined with downclimbing
routes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
routes.descent: Rappel and downclimb to the standard route, then descend

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-serve day-use fee kiosk (Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day); trail departs the north end of the upper Alpental Ski Area parking lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road to its end and park in the upper Alpental lot (~3,100 ft). The trail leaves from the north end of the lot. Self-serve fee kiosk — Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Snow Lake Trail here toward Source Lake and Chair's east basin.
waypoints.directions: The first half mile follows the old ski-area cat track before it becomes standard trail, then climbs gently through forest. Stay on the maintained Snow Lake Trail until the Source Lake fork — that is where you leave it.

waypoints.name: Thumb Tack
waypoints.note: Large rock landmark in Chair's east basin; skis or packs are often cached here before ascending toward the buttress.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the fork and continue cross-country on boot path toward the basin under Chair's east face, roughly half a mile to a mile of talus, heather and (early or mid season) snow. The Thumb Tack is the large rock landmark once you are in the basin; parties commonly cache skis or packs here.

waypoints.name: Buttress base / entry gully
waypoints.note: Blocky entry gully gains low-angle blocky rock leading toward the buttress prow; rope up here for the exposed Class 4 to 5.4 climbing above.
waypoints.directions: From the Thumb Tack climb a short snow gully, about 300 ft, to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress. This gully sits under avalanche terrain coming off Chair and Snoqualmie Mountain and is a known early-season slide path — most parties carry axe and crampons from the basin onward and rope up at the base of the blocky entry gully.

waypoints.name: Tree cluster near buttress prow
waypoints.note: Notable stand of trees used as a belay stance on the ascent and as the first rappel anchor on the descent.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge crest up low-angle blocky rock from the entry gully to the stand of trees on the prow. This is the usual belay stance on the way up, and the first rappel anchor on the way down.

waypoints.name: Chair Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit is the uncorniced center section with rock underneath; the northeast side is heavily corniced.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the buttress — four to five pitches of class 3-4 with big exposure. The true summit is the uncorniced centre section with rock underneath it; the northeast side is heavily corniced, so stay well back from the lip.

waypoints.name: Notch/saddle in main ridge
waypoints.note: Downclimb the SE-facing gully from the true summit to this notch before the rappels; steep unconsolidated snow up to about 70 degrees.
waypoints.directions: Descending: from the true summit, downclimb the southeast-facing gully to the notch in the main ridge. Steep unconsolidated snow, up to roughly 70 degrees.

waypoints.name: Fixed rappel anchor at rock buttress
waypoints.note: Double-rope rappel from a fixed anchor here down to the tree cluster, then continue rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, continue to the fixed anchor on the rock buttress. A double-rope rappel from here reaches the tree cluster, then keep rappelling and downclimbing to the base of the buttress and reverse the approach.

routes.detailed_rack: A single rack of nuts and cams to ~2 in, a few slings/draws, and rappel gear covers the rock route; parties attempting it as a winter line add 2-3 ice screws, a picket or two, and a second tool.
pro_tips: A Cascade classic, popular in both summer and winter
Helmet essential for the variable rock

From the base, follow the blocky gully down-right of the ridge divide, then angle left across slabby ledges to a cluster of trees near the buttress's prow before following the crest to the top — about 400 ft of mostly Class 3-4 with one short 5.4 step.
routes.pro_needs: Placements are sparse on the lower scrambling terrain (roughly 2-3 solid pieces per rope-length); focus small cams and nuts on the steeper pitches, plus ice screws for the crux ice bulge in winter conditions.
routes.best_season: Late July through September for the snow-free rock route; the same buttress is also climbed as a winter ice/mixed line (roughly WI2-3) from about December through March when it's in condition.
routes.approach: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure of the approach gully itself.
routes.descent_text:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

A second gully further along is an alternative rather than a continuation: it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so a single rope is enough to get through that one instead. Anchors on this descent are not maintained and may not be where you want them — carry cord and a knife to re-rig, and expect that getting around remaining steep snow at the base may take an extra downclimb or rappel.

Below the rappel, plunge-step or downclimb 35-40° snow to the base of the east face and traverse east to rejoin the approach. Cornice collapse at the gully lip, sloughing in warm conditions, and rock knocked down by parties above are the main descent hazards.

Rappelling the buttress itself is a documented summer alternative, taking four to five shorter rappels off a tree, a second gnarlier tree, an old pair of bolts and a rock horn.
routes.bail: The lower buttress has natural retreat options (trees, boulders for anchors) - parties can rappel or downclimb back the way they came before committing to the upper ice bulge/steeper pitches. Leave slings/rap rings if bailing mid-route.

Long pitch (70-80m) to the base of the ice bulge.

The second descent gully is an alternative rather than a continuation — it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so one rope suffices there. Rappelling the buttress itself in summer is a separate option again, taking four to five shorter rappels.

approach_variants.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply right from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the north side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and right of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, on snow
approach_variants.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack
